newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nordbanken sees subdued Swedish economy in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Nordbanken sees subdued Swedish economy in 1997.

text.p: One of Sweden's big four banks, Nordbanken, on Wednesday forecast the Swedish economy would be subdued in 1997 but a new boom was around the corner.

It forecast industrial production would rise 2.5 percent in 1997 while Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would grow 1.9 percent, accelerating to a 3.1 percent rise in 1998. Inflation was seen at 1.3 percent in 1997.
Nordbanken said the economic drive would come from stronger European growth and would impact Sweden from 1998.
"The economic recovery in Europe will start next year and really get under way during 1998/99," Nordbanken said in its latest economic forecast.
"Exports will rise by six to seven percent and industrial production by four to five percent a year in the period 1998-2000."
Sweden's continuing high unemployment will continue to weigh down consumption next year but the market would develop further in 1998, Nordbanken said.
"The economic recovery will create more jobs and with that, belief in the future," the bank said.

"The fall in interest rates will increase the value of homes, holiday homes and financial access to shares and bonds, wages will get to keep real increases and worn down capital value will be superseded."
Nordbanken forecast a good outlook for inflation and expected restricted wage increases.

"Employees' inflation expectations for the next two years have now fallen to under two percent and the new agreements should end up at lower levels than those that were made under expectations of an extremely profitable economy with a record low crown and with inflationary expectations of almost four percent," Nordbanken said.
The bank forecast the crown staying steady against the mark at around 4.40 in 1997 and 1998.
It expected the crown to strengthen against the dollar from an average of 6.60 this year to 6.38 in 1997 and 6.17 in 1998.
On unemployment, Nordbanken estimated the number of jobs would increase by 160,000 by the turn of the century.

"The number of people employed will rise on the grounds of the economic recovery, lowering (total) unemployment very moderately from 12.5 percent today to under 10 percent in the year 2000," wrote the bank.
It forecast total unemployment, including those on training and job creation schemes, would rise to 12.7 percent in 1997 but slip back to 12.1 percent in 1998.
It forecast core unemployment, currently running at 7.6 percent, at 7.5 percent next year, 6.3 percent in 1998 and somewhere under six percent by 2000.
Prime Minister Goran Persson has set a goal to cut core unemployment to four percent by 2000.
